title: Our Own Secret Code
bigQuestion: How does a code work, and when is a secret OK to keep?

story.title: Notes About the Cookies
story.kicker: Two sisters send notes in a secret code. Can you find the cookies?
paragraphs: Ana and Lucy are sisters. Grandma baked cookies for the family party. The sisters hid the cookie box as a surprise. Now they want to send notes about it.
Ana draws on a paper. She makes little boxes, corners and dots. It looks like a puzzle. Lucy gets out a card with a tic-tac-toe grid. That card is their key.
Lucy matches each shape to a letter. Slowly, a word appears: SHELF. She smiles. The cookies are on the top shelf! Their brother Leo cannot read the note. He does not have the key.
At the party, the sisters bring out the box. "Surprise!" they shout. Everyone gets a cookie. Mom laughs. "Your secret was a happy one," she says. "Those are the best kind."
story.think: Why could Lucy read the note but Leo could not? What made this a happy secret?

lessons.title: Swap Letters for Shapes
lessons.mainIdea: A code swaps letters for shapes or numbers.
reading: Ben writes his name as 2, 5, 14. Why? B is letter 2. E is letter 5. N is letter 14. He swapped each letter for a number.
A *code* is a way to swap letters for shapes, numbers or other signs. The message stays the same. It just looks different. Only some people can read it.
You can make a code with numbers, colors or little pictures. Each letter gets its own sign. Then you write your message with the signs.

words.d: a way to swap letters for shapes, numbers or other signs

look.title: A Number Name
look.text: Look at this note on the desk: 1, 14, 1. The code is A = 1, B = 2, C = 3, and so on. N is letter 14. So the note spells a short name.
look.prompt: Read the name in the note. Now write your own name with numbers.

check.q: What does a code do?
choices: It swaps letters for shapes or numbers
check.why: The reading says a code swaps letters for shapes, numbers or other signs.

check.q: In Ben's code, what number is the letter B?
check.why: B is the second letter, so Ben writes it as 2.

check.q: What name does the note 1, 14, 1 spell?
check.why: A is 1 and N is 14. So 1, 14, 1 spells ANA.

lessons.title: Every Code Needs a Key
lessons.mainIdea: A key shows which sign goes with which letter.
reading: Lucy has a card that shows each shape and its letter. With the card, she reads Ana's note. Leo has no card. To him, the note is just marks.
The card is called a *key*. A key tells you which sign goes with which letter. With the key, you can read a code. Without it, a code is very hard to read.
Keep your key safe. Share it only with the people you want to read your notes. That is how a code works in a game.

words.d: a list that shows which sign goes with which letter

look.title: Two Friends, One Key
look.text: Look at two friends at a table. Each one has the same small card. The card shows a star for A, a moon for B and a sun for C. A third friend has no card.
look.prompt: Which friends can read a note in star, moon and sun? How could the third friend join the game?

check.q: What does a key show?
choices: Which sign goes with which letter
check.why: The reading says a key tells you which sign goes with which letter.

check.q: Why could Leo not read the note?
check.why: Leo had no card. Without the key, the note is just marks.

check.q: Who should you share your key with?
choices: The people you want to read your notes
check.why: The reading says to share the key only with people you want to read your notes.

lessons.title: Letters in a Grid
lessons.mainIdea: The pigpen code puts letters in a tic-tac-toe grid and an X.
reading: Draw a tic-tac-toe grid. Put A, B and C in the top row. Put D, E and F in the middle. Put G, H and I on the bottom. Now each letter has its own little pen.
This is the *pigpen code*. Each letter is the lines around it. E sits in the middle, so E is a full box. A sits in a corner, so A is just a corner shape.
Two grids and two X shapes hold all 26 letters. Some letters get a dot. The dot tells them apart. The letters sit in pens. That is why we call it pigpen!

words.d: a code that writes each letter as the lines of a grid or X around it
lines that cross to make rows of boxes

look.title: Where the 26 Letters Go
look.cite: The common pigpen key; see Klaus Schmeh, "Ten Peculiar Uses of the Pigpen Cipher," 2016
look.prompt: How many letters go in the two grids? How many go in the two X shapes?

check.q: What shape is the pigpen letter E?
check.why: E sits in the middle of the grid. Lines are all around it, so it is a full box.

check.q: Why is it called the pigpen code?
choices: The letters sit in pens, like pigs
check.why: The letters sit in little pens made by the lines, like pigs in pens.

check.q: What helps tell some pigpen letters apart?
check.why: The reading says some letters get a dot to tell them apart.

lessons.title: Pigpen on Old Stones
lessons.mainIdea: Long ago, people carved pigpen letters on stones.
reading: In New York City, there is an old churchyard. It is called Trinity Churchyard. One stone there is from 1794. It has a line of little boxes, corners and dots.
Those marks are pigpen letters. They are *carved* into the stone. For a long time, people walked by and wondered what they said. Then people used the key and read it.
The stone also shows a square and compass. That tells us the man was a Freemason. Many Freemasons knew the pigpen code long ago.

words.d: a member of an old club that began with stone builders

look.title: A Stone in New York
look.text: An old stone in Trinity Churchyard in New York City is for James Leeson, who died in 1794. It shows a square and compass. It also has a line in pigpen code. Anyone with the key can read it.
look.cite: Atlas Obscura, "Trinity Churchyard" (place entry on the James Leeson stone)
look.prompt: What two kinds of symbols are on the stone? How can a person read the pigpen line?

check.q: In which city is Trinity Churchyard?
check.why: The reading says the old churchyard is in New York City.

check.q: How old is the stone with pigpen letters?
check.why: The stone in Trinity Churchyard is from 1794.

check.q: What else is on the stone besides pigpen letters?
check.why: The stone shows a square and compass, the symbol of the Freemasons.

lessons.title: A Password Shows You Belong
lessons.mainIdea: A password is a secret word that shows you belong to a group.
reading: Kim knocks on the blanket fort. "Password?" asks her brother. "Pancakes!" says Kim. He lets her in. The word shows she is part of the fort club.
A *password* is a secret word that lets you in. Long ago, Scotland had stone builders. They had a secret word too. A builder used it to show he was trained.
Builders also had to remember their lessons. In 1599, a leader made a rule. Each new builder must be tested on his memory. A password is something you keep in your memory.

words.d: a secret word that lets you in or shows you belong
what your mind keeps so you can know it later

look.title: A Rule for Builders, 1599
look.text: In Scotland in 1599, a rule for stone builders said a leader must test every worker and every new learner on how well they remembered their craft.
look.cite: Second Schaw Statutes, 28 December 1599, as printed in The Square magazine
look.prompt: Why would builders want to test what a new worker remembered?

check.q: What was the password for the blanket fort?
check.why: Kim says "Pancakes!" and her brother lets her in.

check.q: What did a stone builder in old Scotland use a secret word for?
check.why: The reading says a builder used the secret word to show he was trained.

check.q: In 1599, what did a rule say new builders must be tested on?
check.why: The 1599 rule said each new builder must be tested on his memory.

lessons.title: Hand Signals
lessons.mainIdea: A hand signal is a sign with your hands that gives a message with no words.
reading: Coach Rivera taps her head. The team knows what it means: run to the base. She does not shout. She uses a *signal*.
A signal is a sign that gives a message. A hand signal uses your hands. A thumbs up can mean good. A raised hand in class can mean I want to talk.
Some clubs have their own handshake. Members know it, and it shows they belong. A handshake or signal is a quiet way to share a message.

words.d: a sign or move that gives a message without words

look.title: Our Quiet Signals
look.text: Picture your classroom. The teacher holds up two fingers. Hands go up for a question. A thumbs up means I am ready. A flat hand on the heart means I need a break.
look.prompt: Make up one hand signal for your class. What message will it give?

check.q: What is a signal?
choices: A sign or move that gives a message
check.why: The reading says a signal is a sign that gives a message.

check.q: What did Coach Rivera's tap on her head mean?
check.why: The team knows her tap means run to the base.

check.q: What can a club's handshake show?
choices: That it is time for lunch
check.why: The reading says a club handshake shows members belong.

lessons.title: Happy Secrets and Unsafe Secrets
lessons.mainIdea: A happy secret is a surprise. An unsafe secret is one you always tell.
reading: Ana and Lucy hid the cookies for a party. Soon everyone knew. That was a *surprise*. A surprise is a happy secret that will be shared soon.
Some secrets are not happy. A secret about someone getting hurt is *unsafe*. A secret about touching or danger is unsafe. So is a secret that makes you feel scared.
Codes and passwords are for fun and games. They are never for hiding something unsafe. You never have to keep an unsafe secret.

words.d: a happy secret that will be shared soon
could hurt someone or put someone in danger

look.title: Sort the Secrets
look.text: Secret 1: We made a birthday card for Dad. Secret 2: Someone said, do not tell that I pushed you. Secret 3: The class password is Pancakes.
look.prompt: Which secrets are happy? Which one is unsafe and must be told to a grown-up?

check.q: What is a surprise?
choices: A secret about someone getting hurt
A secret that makes you scared
A happy secret that will be shared soon
check.why: The reading says a surprise is a happy secret that will be shared soon.

check.q: Which secret is unsafe?
choices: A secret about someone getting hurt
check.why: A secret about someone getting hurt is unsafe. You always tell it.

check.q: What are codes and passwords for?
check.why: The reading says codes and passwords are for fun and games, never for hiding something unsafe.

lessons.title: Tell a Trusted Grown-Up
lessons.mainIdea: If a secret is unsafe, tell a trusted grown-up right away.
reading: Tomas has a secret that makes his tummy feel tight. He goes to his teacher, Ms. Park. He tells her. She listens. She thanks him and helps.
A *trusted grown-up* is an adult who keeps you safe. It can be a parent, a teacher, a school nurse or a counselor. You can tell them anything.
Telling is brave. It is not tattling. If the first grown-up does not help, tell another one. Keep telling until someone helps.

words.d: an adult who listens to you and helps keep you safe

look.title: My Helping Hand
look.text: Trace your hand on paper. On each finger, write or draw one trusted grown-up. One finger could be a parent. One could be a teacher. One could be the school nurse.
look.prompt: Who are five grown-ups you could tell if a secret felt unsafe?

check.q: Who did Tomas tell his secret to?
check.why: Tomas went to his teacher, Ms. Park, and told her.

check.q: What should you do if the first grown-up does not help?
check.why: The reading says to keep telling until someone helps.

check.q: Is telling an unsafe secret tattling?
check.why: The reading says telling is brave. It is not tattling.

review.q: What do you need to read a code?
review.why: A key shows which sign goes with which letter. Without it, a code is hard to read.

review.q: The pigpen code puts letters in what shapes?
choices: A tic-tac-toe grid and an X
review.why: Pigpen puts the letters in two grids and two X shapes.

review.q: Where is an old stone with pigpen letters from 1794?
review.why: The stone in Trinity Churchyard, New York City, is from 1794.

choices: A secret word that shows you belong
review.why: A password is a secret word that lets you in, like Kim's fort password.

review.q: Ana and Lucy hid cookies for a party. What kind of secret was it?
review.why: It was a surprise. Everyone got a cookie at the party.

review.q: A secret makes you feel scared. What should you do?
review.why: An unsafe secret is always told to a trusted grown-up.
